analysis.one_liner: Bars crypto exchanges from lending out or mixing customer money without the customer's consent.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on December 2, 2022, referred to the House Financial Services Committee, never received a hearing or a vote, and died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it illegal for a cryptocurrency exchange to lend out, leverage, or co-mingle (mix with the exchange's own money) a customer's funds unless that customer agreed. It was written in response to the practice that left customers of collapsed crypto firms with nothing when the firms went under. It got no cosponsors, no committee hearing, and no vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People who keep money or crypto on an exchange benefit. The bill would require their consent before the exchange could lend out, leverage, or mix their funds, so their assets could not be quietly used to fund the exchange's own bets. That is the protection that was missing for customers of failed crypto lenders and exchanges, who discovered too late that their deposits had been lent out and were gone.

how_it_helps.text: It bans a cryptocurrency exchange from lending, leveraging, or co-mingling a customer's funds unless that specific customer consents, so customers would know their money is not being lent out or gambled behind their backs.

By default, customer assets would have to stay with the customer, which directly targets the practice that left customers of failed crypto firms as unsecured creditors scrambling for their money back.

analysis.who_pays: Cryptocurrency exchanges pay. They would lose the ability to lend or leverage customer funds by default, which is a profitable use of other people's money, and would have to build consent processes. Customers who currently earn interest on lent-out deposits would lose that option unless they explicitly opted in.

drawbacks.text: The bill is very narrow: it covers only lending, leveraging, and co-mingling of customer funds, and does nothing about the many other ways crypto investors can lose money, such as exchange insolvency, custody failures, or misleading disclosures.

Requiring customer consent before an exchange lends or leverages funds would cut off a revenue source for exchanges and could mean fewer free or discounted services for customers who were willing to accept the risk, and the bill provides no details on how consent must be obtained or enforced.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but narrow: it would stop exchanges from silently lending or gambling with customer money, the practice behind some of the largest crypto losses of 2022. The cost is small and borne mainly by exchanges, which would lose a cheap source of funding and would have to ask customers before using their assets. A fair criticism is that the bill was extremely short and did not address broader risks — custody standards, disclosure, or overall exchange solvency — so even if enacted it would have left most gaps open.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in early December 2022 and sent to the House Financial Services Committee, which never took it up, and it expired when the two-year congressional session ended three weeks into the next January.

narrative.text: Rep. Ritchie Torres introduced the Crypto Consumer Investor Protection Act in the House on December 2, 2022.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services — the only action it ever received.
No other member signed on as a cosponsor.
The committee never held a hearing or markup, and the House never voted; the bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and all unacted bills expire.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Crypto exchanges that lend, leverage, or co-mingle customer funds are better off, because the restriction was never enacted. Ordinary investors who keep money on exchanges remain exposed to the same practices the bill would have banned.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Crypto exchanges that lend customer funds

for.name: Rep. Ritchie Torres
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor; it was referred to the House Financial Services Committee.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Maxine Waters (D-CA)
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill died in committee when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never drew enough engagement to reveal a partisan split: a single Democratic sponsor, zero cosponsors from either party, and no votes or public floor fights.

industries.note: Exchanges would lose the ability to lend, leverage, or mix customer funds for their own trading and lending operations unless each customer consents. That would cut off a major profit source — lending out customer assets — and force exchanges to hold customer money intact, protecting investors from the collapse-style losses of 2022.

Businesses built on borrowing customer crypto to generate yield would lose their default supply of customer funds, since every deposit would have to be left untouched unless the customer agreed otherwise.
